tools.name: Password Strength Checker
tools.summary: Analyze a password in your browser: estimated score, entropy, crack-time ranges, common-password, pattern and repeat checks.
tools.intro: Type a password to see an estimated security score and why it scores that way. Analysis runs locally and the password is never stored or sent anywhere.
notes: The score is our own estimate, not an industry standard, and no score guarantees safety.

faq.a: No. This analysis runs in your browser memory only. The separate breach-check tool is the only one that makes a network request, and it sends just a 5-character hash prefix.

tools.name: Password Breach Check
tools.summary: Check whether a password appears in the Have I Been Pwned dataset using k-anonymity. Only a 5-character hash prefix is sent.
tools.intro: Your password is hashed locally with SHA-1. Only the first five characters of that hash are sent to the Pwned Passwords range API, and the match is made in your browser. This tool needs an internet connection.
notes: Your password is hashed locally. Only the first five characters of the SHA-1 hash are sent for the breach lookup. Your full password and full hash are never sent to the breach-checking service. This tool does make a partial network request.

faq.a: The service returns every hash suffix sharing your 5-character prefix, so it cannot tell which one is yours. You compare the suffix locally.

tools.name: Password Entropy Calculator
tools.summary: Estimate password entropy in bits from length and character pool, with notes on why pattern weaknesses can make the number optimistic.
tools.intro: Entropy estimates unpredictability as H = L × log2(N), where L is length and N the character pool size. It assumes characters were chosen randomly.
notes: Entropy is an estimate. Dictionary words and patterns can make real strength far lower than the character-pool number.

faq.a: The formula assumes random choices. A password like Summer2024! has a large pool but is highly predictable.

tools.name: Password Crack Time Estimator
tools.summary: See rough crack-time ranges for online, offline fast-hash and offline slow-hash attacks. Estimates only, with assumptions explained.
tools.intro: Estimates assume 100 guesses/s online, 10 billion/s against a fast offline hash and 10,000/s against a slow hash, averaging half the search space.
notes: Real cracking time depends on the hash algorithm, attacker hardware, rate limiting, dictionaries, leaked lists and password reuse. Not a guarantee.

faq.a: Attack conditions differ enormously. Rate-limited login pages are slow to attack; a stolen database hashed with a fast algorithm is not.

tools.name: Password Pattern Detector
tools.summary: Detect numeric and alphabetic sequences, keyboard walks, predictable year suffixes and common-password variants locally.
tools.intro: Attackers try predictable patterns first. This tool flags sequences like 1234 or abcd, keyboard runs like qwer, year suffixes and common substitutions.
notes: Detection rules are heuristics and can miss patterns or flag harmless text.

faq.a: Sequences, keyboard runs, trailing years and substitutions like @ for a on a common word.

tools.name: Password Repeat Detector
tools.summary: Find repeated characters and repeated blocks such as aaa, 111, abab or abcabc in a password, entirely in your browser.
tools.intro: Repetition lowers the real number of unpredictable characters. This tool flags repeated characters and repeated blocks.
notes: Heuristic only. A repeat finding means the password is more predictable than its length suggests.

faq.a: They make a password easier to guess and reduce how much of its length actually adds unpredictability.

tools.name: Common Password Checker
tools.summary: Check a password against a built-in list of very common passwords and obvious variants, locally in your browser.
tools.intro: Common passwords are guessed first by attackers. The check is local and covers exact matches and obvious suffix or substitution variants.
notes: The built-in list is small and not complete. Use the breach check for a much larger dataset.

faq.a: No. It covers about fifty very common passwords. The HIBP breach check covers hundreds of millions.

tools.name: Secure Password Generator
tools.summary: Generate strong random passwords with cryptographically secure randomness. Choose length and character sets. Nothing is stored or sent.
tools.intro: Passwords are generated with crypto.getRandomValues, guarantee each selected character type and are shuffled securely.
notes: Store generated passwords in a password manager. This page does not save them.

faq.a: No. They exist only on this page until you close or clear it.

tools.name: Passphrase Generator
tools.summary: Generate memorable multi-word passphrases locally with secure randomness, custom separators and entropy estimates.
tools.intro: Random words are easier to remember than random characters. Words are chosen from a local list with secure randomness.
notes: The built-in list is modest in size, so use 6 or more words for important accounts. Entropy shown is computed from the real list size.

faq.q: How many words should I use?
faq.a: Five to six for most accounts, more for a password-manager master passphrase.

tools.name: Secure PIN Generator
tools.summary: Generate random 4, 6, 8 or 10 digit PINs with secure randomness while avoiding patterns like 1234 or 0000.
tools.intro: PINs are generated with crypto.getRandomValues, and predictable results such as repeats, runs and common patterns are rejected.
notes: Short PINs are weak by nature. Rely on lockouts and rate limiting, and prefer longer PINs.

faq.a: Attackers try the most common PINs first.

tools.name: Random String Generator
tools.summary: Generate random strings from 1 to 256 characters with secure randomness. Choose character sets and exclude ambiguous characters.
tools.intro: Useful for tokens, test data and identifiers. Values come from crypto.getRandomValues.
notes: Do not reuse generated strings across systems and generate real secrets on the server that uses them where possible.

faq.a: The randomness source is suitable, but treat tokens according to your system's own security requirements.

tools.name: UUID v4 Generator
tools.summary: Generate RFC-style version 4 UUIDs in bulk (1, 10, 50 or 100) locally using secure randomness.
tools.intro: UUID v4 values are random 128-bit identifiers with version and variant bits set.
notes: UUIDs are identifiers, not secrets. Do not use them as passwords or access tokens by themselves.

faq.a: Collisions are astronomically unlikely with good randomness.

tools.name: Hash Generator
tools.summary: Generate MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 hashes of any text locally in your browser.
tools.intro: Hashing turns text into a fixed-length fingerprint. Unicode text is hashed as UTF-8 and nothing leaves your browser.
notes: SHA-1 is deprecated for collision resistance. None of these fast hashes are suitable for storing passwords; use bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 instead. MD5 is obsolete for cryptographic security and is included only for checksums and legacy compatibility.

faq.q: Can I hash passwords with this?
faq.a: For checksums yes; for storing passwords no, use a slow password hashing function.

tools.name: Base64 Encoder & Decoder
tools.summary: Encode and decode Base64 with proper UTF-8 handling for Bangla, emoji and other Unicode. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.intro: Base64 represents bytes as text. This tool converts through UTF-8 so non-English text round-trips correctly.
notes: Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Anyone can decode it.

faq.a: Input must be valid Base64 and decode to valid UTF-8 text.

tools.name: QR Code Generator
tools.summary: Create QR codes for text, URLs, Wi-Fi, email and phone numbers entirely in your browser. Download PNG or SVG. Nothing is uploaded.
tools.intro: Enter your content and generate a QR code locally. No QR service is called and your content never leaves your browser.
notes: Your QR content is processed locally in your browser. Wi-Fi QR codes contain the network password in readable form to anyone who scans them, so share them carefully.

faq.q: Is my QR content sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. The QR code is built by code running in your browser, and downloads are created locally.

tools.name: HMAC Generator
tools.summary: Compute and verify HMAC-SHA signatures for messages and webhook payloads, with a constant-time comparison.
tools.intro: Paste the exact message body and the shared secret to compute an HMAC, or paste a received signature to verify it. Prefixes such as sha256= are handled.
notes: Keep secrets private. Verify against the raw body exactly as received, because any whitespace change alters the HMAC.

faq.a: HMAC proves a message came from someone who knows the shared secret and was not changed. Webhook providers use it to sign requests.

tools.name: Symmetric Encrypt / Decrypt (AES-256-GCM)
tools.summary: Encrypt and decrypt text or files with AES-256-GCM and a password, entirely offline in your browser.
tools.intro: Enter a password and your text or file. The key is derived with PBKDF2-SHA-256 (600,000 iterations by default) and every encryption uses a fresh random salt and IV.
notes: Lost passwords cannot be recovered. Files are processed in memory (300 MB limit). Output is only decryptable with this tool's format.

faq.a: No. Encryption uses the Web Crypto API in your browser and nothing is sent anywhere.

tools.name: Key Pair Generator
tools.summary: Generate RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519, ECDH and X25519 key pairs as PEM or JWK, locally in your browser.
tools.intro: Pick an algorithm and generate a key pair with the Web Crypto API. Public keys are exported as SPKI PEM and private keys as PKCS#8 PEM, plus JWK versions.
notes: The private key is shown only on this page and is never stored. Copy it to a secure place. Ed25519 and X25519 need a recent browser.

faq.a: Use Ed25519 or ECDSA P-256 for signatures, X25519 or ECDH for key agreement and RSA-3072 or larger only when you need RSA compatibility.

tools.name: RSA-OAEP Encrypt / Decrypt
tools.summary: Encrypt short messages with an RSA public key and decrypt them with the private key using RSA-OAEP.
tools.intro: Paste a public key (PEM or JWK) to encrypt, or a private key to decrypt Base64 ciphertext. Hash choices are SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512 and SHA-1.
notes: RSA encrypts only small messages (about 190 bytes for RSA-2048 with SHA-256). For larger data, encrypt with AES and protect that key with RSA.

faq.a: Key size in bytes minus twice the hash size minus 2. For RSA-2048 with SHA-256 that is 190 bytes.

tools.name: Digital Signature Tool
tools.summary: Sign messages and verify signatures with ECDSA, Ed25519 or RSA-PSS keys in PEM or JWK form.
tools.intro: Paste a private key to sign or a public key to verify. Signatures are Base64. ECDSA uses the raw r||s encoding used by Web Crypto and JWS.
notes: Never paste a production private key into any website you do not control. This page runs locally, but treat sample keys as disposable.

faq.a: The message, key, hash or algorithm differs from the one used to sign. Even one changed character invalidates a signature.

tools.name: ECDH Key Exchange
tools.summary: Derive a shared secret from your private key and a peer's public key with ECDH or X25519, plus an HKDF key.
tools.intro: Two parties each combine their own private key with the other's public key and get the same secret. The tool also derives a 256-bit key with HKDF-SHA-256.
notes: Use the HKDF output as the key, not the raw shared secret. Key agreement alone does not prove who the other party is.

faq.q: Do both sides get the same secret?
faq.a: Yes. A's private key with B's public key gives the same value as B's private key with A's public key.

tools.name: JWK / PEM Converter
tools.summary: Convert public and private keys between JWK (JSON) and PEM (SPKI or PKCS#8), for RSA, EC, Ed25519 and X25519.
tools.intro: Paste a JWK to get PEM, or a PEM key to get JWK. The direction and key type (public or private) are detected for you.
notes: PKCS#1 (BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY) and SEC1 keys are not accepted; convert them first with openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -nocrypt.

faq.a: SPKI public keys (BEGIN PUBLIC KEY) and PKCS#8 private keys (BEGIN PRIVATE KEY).

tools.name: Key Derivation Tool (PBKDF2, HKDF)
tools.summary: Derive keys with PBKDF2 or HKDF and measure how long your chosen iteration count takes on this device.
tools.intro: PBKDF2 stretches a password into a key; HKDF expands key material you already have. Enter inputs as text or hex and choose the output length.
notes: Use a random salt of at least 16 bytes and a high iteration count for passwords. HKDF is not suitable for low-entropy passwords.

faq.q: How many PBKDF2 iterations should I use?
faq.a: Current guidance for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 is at least 600,000. Use the timing readout to see the cost on your device.

tools.name: Hash Identifier
tools.summary: Identify the likely type of a hash or password-hash string from its format, prefix and length.
tools.intro: Paste a hash and see which algorithms fit, such as bcrypt, Argon2, SHA-crypt, MD5, SHA-1 or SHA-256, with notes on whether they are safe for passwords.
notes: Identification is a heuristic. Many algorithms share a length, so treat the result as a list of candidates, not proof.

faq.a: A 32-character hex string could be MD5, NTLM or MD4. Length alone cannot tell them apart.

tools.name: CRC and Checksum Calculator
tools.summary: Compute CRC-32, CRC-16 (CCITT-FALSE and MODBUS), CRC-8 and Adler-32 checksums of text or hex bytes.
tools.intro: Enter text or hex bytes to get the common checksum variants at once, matching the standard check values.
notes: Checksums catch accidental corruption only. They are not secure against deliberate tampering; use a cryptographic hash or HMAC for that.

faq.a: It is a checksum for error detection, not a cryptographic hash. Anyone can craft data with a chosen CRC.

tools.name: Classical Cipher Tool
tools.summary: Apply Caesar, ROT13, ROT47, Atbash and Vigenere ciphers, or list all 25 Caesar shifts.
tools.intro: A learning tool for historic ciphers and puzzles. Choose a cipher, set the shift or key, and encrypt or decrypt.
notes: These ciphers are trivially broken and offer no real security. Use modern encryption for anything that matters.

faq.a: No. ROT13 only hides text from a casual glance and is undone by applying it again.

tools.name: XOR Cipher Tool
tools.summary: XOR text or hex data with a repeating key, or brute-force a single-byte XOR key by scoring English-like output.
tools.intro: Enter data and a key to get hex output. The brute-force mode tries all 256 single-byte keys and ranks the results.
notes: Repeating-key XOR is not secure encryption. Brute-force scoring suits English text and may miss other data.

faq.a: Only a truly random one-time key as long as the message is secure. A short repeating key is easy to break.

tools.name: SSH Key Fingerprint
tools.summary: Compute the SHA-256 and MD5 fingerprints of an SSH public key, in the format ssh and GitHub display.
tools.intro: Paste one public key line (ssh-ed25519, ssh-rsa or ecdsa) to get its fingerprint for comparing with a server or provider.
notes: Only public keys are needed. Never paste a private key. A matching fingerprint confirms the key, not the person.

faq.q: Where do I find the fingerprint to compare?
faq.a: Run ssh-keygen -lf on the key file, or check the fingerprint shown by your Git host or server on first connection.

tools.name: Merkle Tree Builder
tools.summary: Build a SHA-256 Merkle tree from a list of leaves, get the root, and create or check an inclusion proof.
tools.intro: Enter one leaf per line (text or already-hashed hex). Choose how odd nodes are handled and get the root plus a proof path for any leaf.
notes: Different systems hash leaves and odd nodes differently. Match the convention of the system you are checking.

faq.a: A short list of sibling hashes that lets you recompute the root and prove a leaf is part of the set.

tools.name: Randomness Tester
tools.summary: Run monobit, runs and byte chi-square tests on pasted data or on bytes from the browser's secure generator.
tools.intro: Paste hex or text, or generate bytes with crypto.getRandomValues, and check bit balance, runs and byte frequencies with p-values.
notes: Passing basic tests does not prove cryptographic quality, and a random source will fail about 1 in 100 runs at the 0.01 level by chance.

faq.q: What does a p-value mean here?
faq.a: It is the probability of seeing a result at least this extreme from truly random data. Very small values flag non-random behaviour.

tools.name: TOTP and HOTP Generator
tools.summary: Generate and verify TOTP and HOTP one-time codes from a Base32 secret, with SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512.
tools.intro: Enter the Base32 secret from a 2FA setup to see the live code and the seconds remaining, or verify a code with one step of clock tolerance. Matches RFC 4226 and RFC 6238 test vectors.
notes: Anyone with the secret can generate your codes, so use this for testing and recovery planning, not as a replacement for your authenticator app.

faq.q: Why does my code not match my app?
faq.a: The most common causes are a wrong digit count, period or algorithm, or a device clock that is off by more than 30 seconds.

tools.name: OTPAuth Link and QR Builder
tools.summary: Build an otpauth:// link and QR code for authenticator apps, or parse an existing link into its settings.
tools.intro: Enter the service name, account and a Base32 secret (or generate a random one) to get a link and QR code you can scan with an authenticator app.
notes: The link contains the secret in plain form. Do not share the QR code or link, and delete screenshots after enrolling.

faq.a: Most authenticator apps accept the standard Key URI format, though some ignore non-default algorithms, digits or periods.

tools.name: Password Policy Checker
tools.summary: Test passwords against your own rules for length, character types, banned words, repeats and common passwords.
tools.intro: Set the rules your system uses, paste candidate passwords one per line and see which pass or fail and why. Passwords are not echoed back.
notes: Modern guidance favours length and blocklists over forced complexity. Use this to check what your rules actually allow.

faq.q: Should I require symbols and numbers?
faq.a: Current guidance (for example NIST 800-63B) favours a longer minimum length and blocking known-bad passwords over composition rules.

tools.name: Backup Code Generator
tools.summary: Generate printable sets of random one-time recovery codes without confusing characters like 0, O, 1 and I.
tools.intro: Choose how many codes and how long. Codes use cryptographically secure randomness and a clear alphabet, and are grouped for easy reading.
notes: Store codes offline and treat each as single-use. This tool does not keep them, so save or print them before leaving.

faq.q: How long should recovery codes be?
faq.a: Ten characters from a 30-symbol alphabet is about 49 bits, enough for single-use codes that are also rate-limited.

tools.name: Password Reuse Checker
tools.summary: Compare a list of passwords for exact reuse, near-duplicates and shared chunks without showing the passwords.
tools.intro: Paste your passwords one per line to find reused and look-alike ones such as Summer2024! and Summer2025!. Only line numbers are reported.
notes: Similar passwords are nearly as risky as reused ones: if one leaks, attackers try the variations. Replace them with unique passwords.

faq.q: Is a small change enough to make a password unique?
faq.a: No. Attackers routinely try common mutations such as changing a year, digit or symbol.

tools.name: Login Lockout Calculator
tools.summary: Estimate how long attackers need to guess a PIN or password under your lockout and rate-limit policy.
tools.intro: Enter secret strength and your lockout rules to see guesses per day, the time to exhaust a common-password list and the chance of success over your chosen period.
notes: This is a simple one-account model. Distributed attacks, password spraying and leaked hashes are not covered and can be far faster.

faq.q: What counts as a good lockout policy?
faq.a: One that makes online guessing take years for a strong secret and still blocks the common-password list, combined with blocklists and MFA.

tools.name: Email Alias Generator
tools.summary: Create plus-tag and Gmail dot-variant aliases of your address to separate sign-ups and trace leaks.
tools.intro: Enter your address and tags to get ready-to-use aliases that arrive in the same inbox, or list dot variants for Gmail-style providers.
notes: Not every provider or website supports plus addressing, and aliases do not hide your real address. Use a real forwarding service for that.

faq.q: Do plus aliases protect my privacy?
faq.a: Only partly. They help you filter mail and spot who leaked your address, but the real address is still visible.

tools.name: Password CSV Auditor
tools.summary: Audit an exported password-manager CSV for weak, short, common and reused passwords without displaying the passwords.
tools.intro: Load a CSV exported from a password manager or browser. The tool lists which entries need attention and can download a report that contains no passwords.
notes: The export contains all your passwords in plain text. Audit it, then securely delete the file. Nothing is uploaded.

faq.a: A header row with a password column. Name, URL and username columns are used to label results.

tools.name: MFA Method Advisor
tools.summary: Get a ranked recommendation of multi-factor methods based on account sensitivity, phishing risk and your devices.
tools.intro: Answer a few questions and see passkeys, authenticator apps, push, email and SMS ranked, with the reason for each and what is unavailable to you.
notes: General guidance only. Any second factor is far better than none, and every account should also have backup codes.

faq.q: Is SMS two-factor still worth using?
faq.a: Yes if it is the only option, but it is weaker than authenticator apps or passkeys because of SIM swaps and interception.

tools.name: Hash Wordlist Matcher
tools.summary: Match unsalted MD5 and SHA hashes against your own wordlist to audit weak passwords and solve CTF exercises.
tools.intro: Paste hashes and a wordlist; each word is hashed locally and compared. It shows which hashes appear in your list.
notes: Dictionary lookup only: no brute force, no salts and no slow hashes. Use it for your own data or authorised exercises.

faq.q: Why was my hash not found?
faq.a: Either the plaintext is not in your list, the hash is salted or slow (such as bcrypt), or it uses an unsupported length.
